summary: Single-author (LinearB) workshop paper proposing 'mise en place' for agentic coding: three phase-gated preparation steps before agents write code (externalize tacit domain knowledge into briefing documents, co-write a specification with an agent, decompose it into dependency-aware task records with acceptance criteria) and the notion of 'context fluency' as a developer skill. The only evidence is the author's own five-hour hackathon: about 2 hours of preparation (10 docs, 9,386 words; 64 task records), then four parallel subagents built an 8,496-line TypeScript education platform with no architectural refactoring. There is no control condition, the competition outcome is not reported, and the model is never named.

claims.claim: About two hours of preparation enabled rapid parallel implementation by concurrent agents
claims.evidence: Table 1 and Fig. 2: 43 of 64 task records closed, median 5.9 min each, 184 min of agent implementation, 9 deploy commits. No comparison condition; the 11 other teams were not instrumented and the hackathon result is not reported.

claims.claim: Near-zero architectural rework is consistent with rich upfront context reducing agent misalignment
claims.evidence: Author's own observation that post-build bugs were integration and styling issues; the paper itself says causation cannot be established from one case.

claims.claim: Twenty minutes of dictated pedagogical intuition substantially reduced iteration on the tutor component
claims.evidence: No iteration count, comparison or measurement of the tutor component is reported.

claims.claim: Preparation-first workflows front-load alignment work that iterative 'vibe coding' pays later as rework
claims.evidence: Argument only; the paper lists this as open research question RQ1 and states there was no iteration-first comparison.

patterns.note: Phase 1 'contextual grounding' (API exploration notes, competitive analysis, dictated tacit knowledge) precedes the specification. One uncontrolled case by the author; no comparison against starting without it.
Markdown briefing documents encoding domain knowledge and design philosophy serve as persistent agent context. Not compared with a no-briefing run.
Collaborative specification through human-agent dialogue, with value judgments encoded as constraints. No comparison.

The spec is decomposed into 64 dependency-tagged task records (Beads; authorship split between human and agent unclear) and dispatched to four parallel subagents. Median 5.9 min per record; no comparison with any other decomposition or a single agent.
Task records carry acceptance criteria; not evaluated.
In Phase 2 the agent proposes details for the human to accept or reject; agent-initiated clarifying questions are neither specified nor measured.
'Context fluency' is proposed as a developer skill to teach and hire for; developer comprehension or deskilling is not measured.

methodology.sample: One practitioner (the author), one five-hour hackathon, one product
methodology.baselines: None; 11 other teams described qualitatively from public pitches and event observation

standards.peer_review: Accepted at the VibeX 2026 workshop (co-located with EASE 2026), 5 pages
standards.artifacts: Zenodo bundle (anonymized hackathon artifacts, MIT-licensed code), doi 10.5281/zenodo.19868258

biases.detail: n=1 practitioner, n=1 project, five hours.
The author evaluates his own method on his own project using his own observations.
Timings and 'near-zero rework' come from the author's own logs and judgment.
Operator expertise in both education and software engineering is an acknowledged confound.
The paper concedes the ingredients are established (Research-Plan-Implement, Spec Kit, Beads); the culinary framing and 'context fluency' rename known practice.
No model, token or cost information.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None of LinearB's products; third-party open-source Beads is used
coi.detail: Vendor affiliation without evaluating a vendor product. The main bias is the author grading his own method.

verdict_reason: A practice proposal backed by a single uncontrolled self-report with no outcome measure; the efficacy statements are unsupported by the body. The gate rejects at rigor 1. The method description itself is on-topic and can inform hypotheses, not decisions.
applicability: On-topic as a practice description: write domain briefing documents before the spec, co-author the spec with the agent, decompose into dependency-tagged tasks with acceptance criteria. The team could trial the 'dictate tacit domain knowledge into a briefing file' step for cross-repository work rules and content conventions, but this paper gives no evidence that it helps; the matched preparation-first vs iteration-first comparison (its RQ1) is what the team would have to run itself. A five-hour greenfield hackathon by one expert does not resemble multi-repo Java service evolution by developers who lack domain knowledge.

conflicts_with.detail: DAGent reports that growing the plan as evidence arrives beats committing a full plan upfront and patching it (deep-research tasks); Mise en Place prescribes completing all preparation phases before implementation. Different domain, and Mise en Place has no comparison.

SWE-WebDev Bench argues closed-loop planning-execution feedback matters more than any upfront phase; Mise en Place insists on phase-gated preparation completed before implementation. Neither has controlled evidence.
